# Reasoning Models and Test-Time Compute {#sec-reasoning}

@sec-post-training ended with a model that had been taught to answer. This
chapter is about a second dial, discovered later and priced differently: not
*how much you train*, but **how much the model is allowed to compute when the
question arrives**.

It is the first dial in this book that you turn at *run time*, on a per-request
basis, for money you spend that same second. That makes it the first one an
engineer can get badly wrong in production without ever running a training job.

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain why writing intermediate tokens gives a transformer more computation,
  and why that is a claim about *architecture* rather than about *thinking*;
- distinguish chain-of-thought as a prompting trick from chain-of-thought as a
  trained behaviour, and say what reinforcement learning changed;
- price a thinking budget in cost per correct answer, not accuracy alone, and
  find the point where the curve stops paying;
- choose between spending test-time compute sequentially, in parallel, or under
  a verifier;
- name the task types where reasoning reliably helps and the ones where it only
  burns tokens — from a measurement, not a hunch;
- treat a reasoning trace as evidence with a known, measured unreliability.

## Why writing more tokens buys more computation {#sec-why-tokens-compute}

Start with the mechanism, because everything else in the chapter is a
consequence of it, and because the usual explanation — "the model thinks out
loud" — explains nothing.

A transformer has a fixed number of layers. @sec-transformers built one: an
embedding, $L$ identical blocks, an output head. When the model produces a
token, the computation that produced it is exactly $L$ blocks deep. Not
adaptive, not conditional on difficulty. **A hard question gets the same number
of layers as an easy one.**

So consider a model that must answer `48 + 48/2` in a single token. Everything
— parse, divide, add — has to happen inside those $L$ blocks, in one pass. If
the problem needs more sequential steps than the model has layers, there is
nowhere to put them.

Now let it write first. Each token it generates is appended to the context and
fed back in, so producing the *next* token is another $L$ blocks — and those
blocks can attend to the tokens just written. Two things change at once, and
only the first is usually mentioned:

1. **Serial depth.** $n$ generated tokens give roughly $n \times L$ blocks of
   sequential computation instead of $L$.
2. **Working memory.** Between one position and the next a transformer carries
   forward exactly one thing: the per-position states of the tokens already
   written, which later positions read back through attention. There is no
   register file and no scratchpad off to the side. So writing `24` down does
   two jobs at once — it fixes the value for later steps to read, and it buys
   one more position's worth of state to compute in. Not written, not
   available.[^filler]

[^filler]: Strictly, what attention reads at an earlier position is that
position's hidden state, not the characters `24`, and a hidden state can hold
more than the token spells out. @pfau2024letsthink pushes precisely on that gap:
transformers given purpose-built supervision can solve problems using **filler**
tokens — literally `...` — hitting "100% and 94% accuracy" on two synthetic
tasks they otherwise fail. Two limits keep this a footnote rather than a
correction. It does not arise from ordinary training — "standard
chain-of-thought data is insufficient for models to learn to leverage filler
tokens effectively", and commercial models "achieve the same performance with
filler tokens as they do when responding directly". And it is bounded:
"transformers remain in TC⁰ with even a polynomial number of filler tokens", so
filler buys extra width *within* a complexity class where chain-of-thought buys
serial depth *beyond* it. It earns its place here for a different reason
entirely — see @sec-faithfulness — as a clean demonstration that the computation
and the text describing it can come apart completely.

The bottom row is not a metaphor for thinking. It is the same network, run more
times, with its own output as input. That is the whole of test-time compute —
and it is why the rest of this chapter can talk about buying accuracy with
tokens as if it were a purchase, because it is one.
:::
::::

Two consequences fall straight out of this picture, and both matter later.

**A trace can be wrong in its wording and still help.** If what pays is the
extra serial computation and the values written down, then prose that
misdescribes the computation can still sit alongside a correct answer. Hold on
to this; @sec-faithfulness is where it stops being a curiosity and becomes a
governance problem.

**More tokens cannot help a problem that was never depth-limited.** If the
answer needed one pass, the extra passes have nothing to do. That is not a
prediction; @sec-cot-limits measures it.

## Chain-of-thought: prompted, then trained {#sec-cot-two-ways}

### The prompting era

In 2022 the finding was that you could get this behaviour for free, from a
model nobody had trained for it. @wei2022chain showed that few-shot prompts
whose worked examples included the intermediate steps changed the outputs
sharply: PaLM 540B on GSM8K went from **17.9%** with standard prompting to
**56.9%** with chain-of-thought — the paper's own delta, $+39.0$ points.

::: {#gloss-chain-of-thought .column-margin .term-gloss}
**chain-of-thought** — intermediate steps a model writes before its final
answer. Originally a prompting pattern; now, in reasoning models, a trained
behaviour with its own token block.
[↩](#term-chain-of-thought){.term-back}
:::

@kojima2022zeroshot then removed even the examples. Appending
`Let's think step by step` to the question took text-davinci-002 on GSM8K from
**10.4%** to **40.7%**. A sentence, worth thirty points.

Two things about that era are easy to forget, and both are in @wei2022chain
explicitly. First, it was
[chain-of-thought](#gloss-chain-of-thought){#term-chain-of-thought .term-ref}
as an *emergent* effect: "chain-of-thought prompting is an emergent ability of
model scale". The paper gives two different thresholds, and they are worth
keeping apart. Gains arrive late: prompting "does not positively impact
performance for small models, and only yields performance gains when used with
models of $\sim$100B parameters". Harm arrives much earlier — "chain of thought
actually hurts performance for most models smaller than 10B
parameters".[^wei-scale] Small models produce fluent, confident, wrong steps.
Second, it was a
*prompting* result. The weights knew nothing about it. You were asking a model
to imitate a **form** it had seen in pretraining: worked solutions, textbook
derivations, StackExchange answers.

[^wei-scale]: The $\sim$100B figure is from their §3.2, the 10B figure from
Appendix A.1; between the two lies a band where chain-of-thought is neither
reliably helpful nor reliably harmful. Note that no model in the sweep sits at
100B — the ladder runs GPT-3 at 350M/1.3B/6.7B/175B, LaMDA at
422M/2B/8B/68B/137B and PaLM at 8B/62B/540B, so the turn is *bracketed*
(between 8B and 62B for PaLM, 68B and 137B for LaMDA) rather than located. The
threshold is task-dependent too: gains are "larger ... for more-complicated
problems", and on SingleOp, the single-step subset of MAWPS, improvements "were
either negative or very small".

Imitating the form has a specific weakness. Nothing in the objective rewards
the steps for being *correct*, or for being the steps that actually produced
the answer. It rewards them for looking like the steps in the prompt.

### What reinforcement learning changed

The 2024–2025 shift was to stop asking and start training. @sec-preference built the
machinery: sample, score, update. Replace the human preference score with an
**automatic check of the final answer** — did the program pass its tests, is
the number right — and you can run that loop at a scale no human labelling
budget reaches.

::: {#gloss-verifiable-reward .column-margin .term-gloss}
**verifiable reward** — a training signal computed by checking the answer
automatically, rather than by asking a human or a learned reward model. It
works only where correctness is cheap to check.
[↩](#term-verifiable-reward){.term-back}
:::

The published account to read is DeepSeek-R1 [@guo2025deepseekr1], because it
is the one that shows its work. Their DeepSeek-R1-Zero was trained by
reinforcement learning from a base model with **no supervised warm-up at all**,
on a [verifiable reward](#gloss-verifiable-reward){#term-verifiable-reward .term-ref}. Over training, its
average pass@1 on AIME 2024 rose **from 15.6% to 77.9%**; with self-consistency
decoding — a technique @sec-parallel-compute returns to — it reached 86.7%.

What makes this different in kind from prompting is *where the behaviour comes
from*. Nobody demonstrated backtracking. The reward said only "the final answer
was right", and the strategies that produce right answers were discovered.
The paper reports an "aha moment" during training, and is refreshingly concrete
about what that means empirically: it is "characterized by a sudden increase in
the use of the word 'wait'". The model taught itself to stop and re-check.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The honest footnote on R1-Zero.** Pure RL from a base model did not produce a
shippable assistant. The same paper reports that R1-Zero "faces challenges such
as poor readability and language mixing, occasionally combining English and
Chinese in a single CoT response", and that its rule-based RL stage was
"narrowly focused on reasoning tasks", leaving it weak at writing and
open-domain questions. The released DeepSeek-R1 adds supervised stages around
the RL to fix exactly this.

The lesson generalises past this one model: **a reward that only checks the
answer only constrains the answer.** Everything you did not measure is free to
drift — which is @sec-forgetting's point arriving from a new direction.
:::

OpenAI's o1 [@openai2024o1] made the commercial case at the same time, with the
figure caption that named the two dials: "o1 performance smoothly improves with
both train-time and test-time compute". Be precise about what is public here,
because a lot of writing is not: OpenAI published *results*, not a method. The
only methodological statement is that a large-scale reinforcement learning
algorithm teaches the model to use its chain of thought. No algorithm, no
reward model, no data. They also chose not to show raw traces to users, citing
"user experience, competitive advantage, and the option to pursue the chain of
thought monitoring" — so what a user sees in the product is a *summary* of the
trace, not the trace.

Both columns end in tokens that look alike, and that resemblance is what makes
the distinction easy to miss. The difference shows up under pressure: prompted
reasoning degrades when you reword the prompt, because the form was never in
the weights.

## Thinking budgets, latency, and the shape of the cost curve {#sec-budgets}

A reasoning model does not just produce more tokens. It produces them in a
structurally separate place — a block, delimited, generated before the answer
and usually hidden from the person who asked. That structure is what makes a
**budget** possible: you can cap the block without touching the answer.

Qwen3 makes the two modes explicit enough to experiment on, which is why this
chapter uses it. Its chat template carries an `enable_thinking` flag. With it
on, the model opens a `<think>` block, reasons, closes it, and answers. With it
off, the template inserts an *empty* `<think></think>` pair, so the model skips
straight to the answer. **Same weights, two behaviours.**

Resist the temptation to call that a controlled experiment. The weights are
held fixed, which is more than most comparisons manage, but three things still
move with the switch: the prompt differs by the injected tag, the two modes were
*both* trained deliberately so neither is a neutral baseline, and — the one that
actually bites — Qwen3 ships different recommended sampling settings for each
mode, which we follow.[^decode] Read the comparisons below as *thinking mode
versus non-thinking mode, each run the way its authors intend it to be run*.
That is the choice a practitioner faces. It is not the same as isolating a
single variable, and no result in this chapter depends on pretending otherwise.

[^decode]: Thinking mode runs at temperature 0.6, top-$p$ 0.95, top-$k$ 20;
non-thinking at temperature 0.7, top-$p$ 0.8, top-$k$ 20. These are the model
card's per-mode recommendations. The practical consequence is that the
no-thinking row of the table below is not *only* a no-thinking row — it also
samples a little hotter and truncates the tail harder, and we have not
separated those effects from the absence of the block.

::: {#gloss-thinking-budget .column-margin .term-gloss}
**thinking budget** — a cap on how many tokens a model may spend inside its
reasoning block before it must produce an answer. Hitting the cap does not
cancel the request; it forces the answer out of an unfinished trace.
[↩](#term-thinking-budget){.term-back}
:::

::: {.fig-cap}
Panel B is what a *hard* budget does — the kind our harness implements, and the
worst case any gentler implementation is measured against. Be precise about the
failure it creates: the request is not cancelled and no error is raised. An
answer comes back, on time, from an unfinished derivation. That failure mode is
invisible in your latency dashboard and invisible in your error rate.
:::
::::

### What you are actually paying for

Three separate costs move together when the block gets longer, and they are
charged to three different people.

**Tokens.** The tokens inside the block are generated like any others. On a
hosted API they land in your output-token count even though your user never
reads them; on your own hardware they occupy your accelerator for the same
duration. Hidden is not free — it is only *invisible*.

**Latency.** This is the one that surprises teams. No *answer* token exists
until the block closes. At a serving throughput of $T$ tokens per second, a
2,000-token trace is $2000/T$ seconds before the first word of the answer.
Streaming does not fix this, because there is no answer to stream yet.

Whether the user stares at a blank screen for that whole interval is a separate,
product-level decision, and it varies by provider. Anthropic's streaming API
emits the trace live as `thinking_delta` events; DeepSeek streams it in a
separate `reasoning_content` field; OpenAI's o-series does not expose the raw
trace at all, only an optional summary. So you may have the *option* of showing
something — a scrolling trace, a summary, or a spinner. What no provider can
give you is the answer sooner.

**Context.** The trace competes for the same window as everything else. In a
multi-turn agent that keeps its own traces, a reasoning model eats its context
several times faster than a non-reasoning one.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The metric to put on the dashboard is not accuracy.** It is **cost per
correct answer** — tokens spent divided by problems solved. Accuracy alone is
monotone-ish and tells you to always spend more; cost per correct answer has a
minimum, and that minimum is the number you are actually looking for.
:::

### Measuring the curve

Everything from here is measured, on a laptop, with a script you can rerun.
The instrument is **Qwen3-1.7B** (1,720,574,976 parameters, bfloat16, Apple
MPS). The task is **GSM8K** [@cobbe2021training], grade-school word problems
whose answers are single numbers — so scoring is exact, with no judge model in
the loop. We sample 200 problems from the test split with a fixed seed.

For each problem we sweep a
[thinking budget](#gloss-thinking-budget){#term-thinking-budget .term-ref}
across 0, 128, 256, 512, 1,024 and 2,048 tokens. Budget 0 means
`enable_thinking=False`: the same weights, answering directly. Every other
budget runs in two phases, and the mechanism matters for how you read the
results:

```text
phase 1   generate with stop_strings=["</think>"], max_new_tokens=budget
          → if the model closed the block itself, it finished thinking
          → if it hit the cap, we close the block for it

phase 2   feed prompt + trace + "\n</think>\n\n" back in, generate the answer
          (capped at 320 tokens — see the caveat below)
```

**Be precise about what this measures.** Phase 1 is a guillotine: at token $N$
the trace stops, mid-sentence, and the block is closed on the model's behalf.
That is the *harshest* possible reading of the word "budget", and it is
deliberately not what the major hosted APIs do. Anthropic's docs say plainly
that "the budget is a target rather than a strict cap"; Google's say the model
"might overflow or underflow the token budget"; OpenAI's `reasoning_effort` is
not a token count at all. What none of them document is the interesting half —
what happens when a model *would* run past the number — so whether the ceiling
is enforced by truncation, by training, or by something else is not a thing you
can learn from the documentation.[^budget-api]

So read the numbers below as a **bound, not an estimate**: this is how much
accuracy a naive cap costs, which is the worst case a smarter implementation is
measured against. We record how often the cap was hit, because a budget that
truncates 90% of traces and a budget that truncates 5% of them are different
regimes wearing the same number.

[^budget-api]: Two further reasons not to map our budgets onto an API call.
First, the small end of our sweep is below what the hosted parameters would even
accept — Anthropic enforces a 1,024-token minimum on `budget_tokens`, so our
128 and 256 rows have no API equivalent. Second, the parameter itself is on its
way out: `budget_tokens` is deprecated on the Claude 4.6 models and rejected
outright by 4.7 and later in favour of `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` with an
`effort` setting, and Gemini's `thinkingBudget` has likewise been superseded by
`thinkingLevel`. The industry is moving from *you pick the number* to *the model
picks and you pick the appetite* — which makes the shape of the curve more
useful to know than any particular vendor's spelling of it.

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**A limitation we found by checking our own instrument, and did not fix.**
Scoring uses the GSM8K convention: the model's answer is the *last number it
writes*. That rule is standard and mostly fine, but it has a failure mode —
anything the model adds after its answer captures the score. "The answer is 72.
Note this assumes 3 items" is read as **3**, and marked wrong.

Which makes the 320-token ceiling on the answer phase more interesting than it
should be. Measured mean answer lengths come out between 243 and 276 tokens
against that ceiling, and a mean that close to a hard cap means a real share of
answers are running into it and being cut mid-sentence — where the last number
is whatever digit the truncation happened to land on. We did not record the
exact fraction on this sweep, which was a mistake in experiment design rather
than an interesting property of the model.

And it is worse than a uniform tax, which is the part worth slowing down for.
Mean answer length is **lowest in the no-thinking row** (243 tokens) and higher
in *every* thinking row (276, 267, 260, 273, 275). The penalty therefore falls
hardest on exactly the rows being compared against the baseline, and lightest on
the baseline itself — so whatever this artefact is doing, it is doing more of it
to thinking than to not-thinking.

What we cannot do is sign the correction. Those five numbers do not move
monotonically with the budget, and neither does accuracy, so there is no clean
story of the form "the bias shrinks as the curve climbs, therefore the true gap
is larger than it looks". All we can say is that the rows are not equally
affected, that the direction of the net distortion is unknown, and that some
unidentifiable part of this curve's shape belongs to our instrument rather than
to the model. The two cannot be separated from what we saved.

We are reporting this rather than quietly raising the cap and re-running,
because noticing that your measuring instrument has a bias is the normal
condition of doing this work, and a chapter that only ever shows clean results
would teach you the wrong lesson about what evaluation feels like. The
practical fix is one line — record whether each answer hit the ceiling, the way
we already record it for traces — and it is in the lab at the end of the
chapter so you do not repeat the mistake.
:::

Here is the sweep. Two hundred GSM8K problems, six budgets, one model, one
laptop, about seven hours of wall time.

| thinking budget | accuracy | 95% CI | thinking tokens | answer tokens | total | traces cut off |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| none (`enable_thinking=False`) | 70.0% | 63.3–75.9 | 0 | 243 | 243 | — |
| 128 tokens | 61.0% | 54.1–67.5 | 125 | 276 | 401 | 97% |
| 256 tokens | 63.5% | 56.6–69.9 | 249 | 267 | 516 | 97% |
| 512 tokens | **71.5%** | 64.9–77.3 | 495 | 260 | 755 | 96% |
| 1,024 tokens | 67.5% | 60.7–73.6 | 920 | 273 | 1193 | 67% |
| 2,048 tokens | 70.0% | 63.3–75.9 | 1362 | 275 | 1637 | 28% |

Read the last row against the first before anything else. At a 2,048-token
budget the model scores **70.0%**. With thinking switched off entirely it scores
**70.0%**. The same two hundred problems, the same weights, the same seed — and
**6.74× the tokens** for a difference of exactly zero.

That is the whole chapter in two rows.

**Now the discipline.** It would be easy to narrate the middle of this table: a
dip at 128, a recovery, a peak at 512, a wobble. Do not. Run the numbers against
the noise and every one of those stories dissolves:

```text
vs no-thinking baseline, two-proportion z-test (n=200 each)
  budget   128:  z = -1.89   NOT separable
  budget   256:  z = -1.38   NOT separable
  budget   512:  z = +0.33   NOT separable
  budget  1024:  z = -0.54   NOT separable
  budget  2048:  z = +0.00   NOT separable
```

**Not one budget is distinguishable from not thinking at all.** The 95% interval
on every row is about $\pm 7$ points wide, and every row's interval contains
every other row's estimate. The 512 row is bolded because it is the largest
number in the column, not because it is the best budget — at $z = +0.33$ that
bolding is decoration, and you should read it with suspicion.[^paired-test]

[^paired-test]: The $z$-test above is the *wrong* test, and wrong in the
    conservative direction. Every budget saw the same 200 problems in the same
    order, so this is a paired design and McNemar's test — which conditions on
    the problems the two conditions disagree about, and discards the large
    majority they both get right — would have more power. We report $z$ because
    our result files saved only the per-budget mean, which throws the pairing
    away. The lab and the published script both record per-problem correctness
    so you are not stuck with our mistake. Note the direction: a more sensitive
    test could only *narrow* these gaps into significance, never widen them, so
    "not separable" is the weakest form of this chapter's claim, not the
    strongest.

**What *is* solidly measured is the cost, and the truncation.** Those columns are
not proportions of 200 coin flips; they are means over hundreds of thousands of
tokens, and they are sharp:

- **Tokens grow monotonically and steeply:** 1.00×, 1.65×, 2.12×, 3.11×, 4.91×,
  6.74×. There is nothing ambiguous about the bill.
- **The truncation rate collapses in exactly the right place:** 97%, 97%, 96%,
  67%, 28%. Below 512 tokens this model is essentially *never* allowed to finish
  a thought. At 2,048 most traces close on their own.

Put those two together and the shape of the accuracy column stops being
mysterious. The rows where accuracy sits *below* the baseline (128 and 256) are
precisely the rows where 97% of traces are guillotined mid-derivation. The row
that finally lets two thirds of traces finish (2,048) lands exactly back on the
baseline. A hard budget that truncates almost everything is not "less thinking" —
it is a different and worse operation, one that hands the answer phase a
half-finished derivation and asks it to commit.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why this is not a failure of the experiment.** A reader hoping for a tidy
rising curve will find this table disappointing, and that reaction is worth
examining, because the result is not weak — it is *precise about the right
thing*. We can state with confidence that on this task, with this model, at this
sample size, buying up to 6.74× more tokens purchased **no detectable accuracy at
all**, and we can put a bound on how large an effect we could have missed: at
$n=200$, roughly 13 points. Anything smaller than that was never visible to this
experiment, and anything larger would have shown up.

That is a genuinely useful finding to carry into a procurement conversation. "It
might help a little, we cannot tell, and here is the bill" is the honest answer,
and it is the one most reasoning-model deployments actually deserve.
:::

### Pricing it yourself

Accuracy per token is a property of the model and the task. Cost per correct
answer is a property of *your* prices and *your* hardware, so the last step has
to be a calculator rather than a claim. The measured points below are ours; the
two sliders are yours.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
budgetRows = [
  {budget: 0, acc: 70.0, total_tok: 243, capped: 0},
  {budget: 128, acc: 61.0, total_tok: 401, capped: 97},
  {budget: 256, acc: 63.5, total_tok: 516, capped: 97},
  {budget: 512, acc: 71.5, total_tok: 755, capped: 96},
  {budget: 1024, acc: 67.5, total_tok: 1193, capped: 67},
  {budget: 2048, acc: 70.0, total_tok: 1637, capped: 28}
]
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tokPrice = Inputs.range([0.05, 20], { value: 2.0, step: 0.05, label: "Price per 1M output tokens (USD)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof tps = Inputs.range([10, 600], { value: 120, step: 5, label: "Single-request decode speed (tokens/second)" })
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
budgetCost = budgetRows.map(d => {
  const costPer1k = (d.total_tok * 1000 * tokPrice) / 1e6;
  const solved1k = (d.acc / 100) * 1000;
  return {
    ...d,
    label: d.budget === 0 ? "no thinking" : `${d.budget.toLocaleString()} tokens`,
    costPer1k,
    perCorrect: solved1k > 0 ? costPer1k / solved1k : NaN,
    latency: d.total_tok / tps
  };
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 680,
  height: 320,
  marginLeft: 66,
  marginBottom: 46,
  x: { label: "average tokens generated per problem", grid: true },
  y: { label: "USD per correct answer", grid: true, zero: true },
  marks: [
    Plot.line(budgetCost, { x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", stroke: "#DDE2E7", strokeWidth: 2 }),
    Plot.dot(budgetCost, {
      x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", r: 5,
      fill: d => d.perCorrect === d3.min(budgetCost, v => v.perCorrect) ? "#B3453E" : "#1F4E79",
      title: d => `${d.label}\n${d.acc.toFixed(1)}% correct\n${d.total_tok.toFixed(0)} tokens\n$${d.perCorrect.toFixed(4)} per correct answer`
    }),
    Plot.text(budgetCost, {
      x: "total_tok", y: "perCorrect", text: "label",
      dy: -14, fontSize: 11, fill: "#5B6272"
    })
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
html`<table style="width:100%; border-collapse:collapse; font-size:0.95rem">
  <tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #DDE2E7">
    <th style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:left">budget</th>
    <th style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">accuracy</th>
    <th style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">USD / 1,000 requests</th>
    <th style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">USD / correct answer</th>
    <th style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">seconds / request</th>
  </tr>
  ${budgetCost.map(d => html`<tr style="${
      d.perCorrect === d3.min(budgetCost, v => v.perCorrect)
        ? "background:#FBF1F0; font-weight:600" : ""}">
    <td style="padding:6px 10px">${d.label}</td>
    <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">${d.acc.toFixed(1)}%</td>
    <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">$${d.costPer1k.toFixed(2)}</td>
    <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">$${d.perCorrect.toFixed(4)}</td>
    <td style="padding:6px 10px; text-align:right">${d.latency.toFixed(1)}</td>
  </tr>`)}
</table>
<p style="font-size:0.85rem; color:#5B6272; margin-top:8px">
The highlighted row is the cheapest correct answer at the current prices. Both
the accuracy and the token counts are measured; only the price and the decode
speed are yours to set. Note what the price slider cannot change: it scales
every row identically, so <b>the cheapest budget does not move as the price
moves</b>. It depends on the shape of the accuracy curve. What the price changes
is how much the wrong choice costs you.
<br><br>
That invariance is real but narrow, and it is worth knowing where it breaks.
This model charges for output tokens only. Add anything that does <i>not</i>
grow with the budget — input tokens, a per-request fee, a retrieval call — and
the fixed part dilutes the variable part, which pushes the optimum towards
longer budgets. Likewise the seconds column is decode time for one request in
isolation: under batching, throughput per request falls while tokens per second
across the fleet rises, so treat it as a lower bound on latency rather than a
capacity estimate.</p>`
```

::: {.callout-caution appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**One task, one model, one prompt format.** This curve is Qwen3-1.7B on GSM8K,
and it is worth being explicit that **we did not get the textbook shape**. The
canonical picture — cheap early gains, a knee, then a flat tail — is what the
literature reports for large models. Our small model instead spent its first
three budgets *below* the baseline and its last one exactly on it.

That is not a contradiction of the literature; it is the same finding from the
other side of the scale threshold. Recall from @sec-cot-two-ways that
chain-of-thought "actually hurts performance for most models smaller than 10B
parameters" — and this is a 1.7B model. What our truncation column adds is a
concrete mechanism for the harm: at the budgets where accuracy fell, 97% of
traces were being severed mid-derivation.

So take two things from this table and leave the third. Take the *method*, and
take the discovery that the honest answer can be "no detectable difference, at
this price". Do not take the location of a knee — we did not find one, and on
your task and model you may well find that the curve genuinely climbs.
@sec-cot-limits runs the same sweep on a task where it should not.
:::
## Spending the budget sideways: self-consistency, verifiers, and search {#sec-parallel-compute}

@sec-budgets bought computation in one direction only: a longer trace. But a
token budget is just a quantity, and there is a second thing you can do with it.
Instead of one 2,000-token attempt, take **eight 250-token attempts and combine
them**. Same tokens, same bill, completely different failure profile.

This is the axis most teams never try, and it is often the better buy.

### Why more attempts help at all

The reason is a property of *errors*, not of models, and it is worth stating
precisely because it also tells you when the trick fails.

Sample the same problem several times at a non-zero temperature and you get
different reasoning paths. Now notice the asymmetry:

- There is usually **one way to be right**. Every path that reasons correctly
  lands on the same number.
- There are **many ways to be wrong**. A dropped sign, a misread quantity, an
  arithmetic slip in step four — each produces a *different* wrong number.

So correct answers pile up on one value while wrong answers scatter. Taking the
majority is therefore not a vote about quality; it is exploiting the fact that
**agreement is evidence and disagreement is noise**. @wang2023selfconsistency
named this *self-consistency*, and it is the reason a model can be right more
often than its single best guess.

Say that backwards, because the backwards form is the operational one: **if your
task's wrong answers can agree with each other, self-consistency will confidently
amplify the error.** A model with a systematic bias — a units convention it
always misreads, a Turkish negation suffix it always misses — votes for the same
wrong answer eight times out of eight. Majority voting turns a 60%-confident
mistake into a 100%-confident one. You get no warning; the votes look unanimous.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}
<div class="fig-title">Two ways to spend the same token budget</div>
<svg viewBox="0 0 764 446" style="max-width:744px" role="img"
     aria-label="A comparison of sequential and parallel test-time compute under an equal token budget of two thousand tokens. On the left, sequential: one question feeds a single long reasoning trace of two thousand tokens which produces one answer. Its properties are that depth accumulates so later steps can build on earlier ones, that an error early in the trace is inherited by everything after it, that latency is the full length of the trace, and that it needs no way of comparing answers. On the right, parallel: the same question is sampled eight independent times at a non-zero temperature, each trace two hundred and fifty tokens, producing eight candidate answers. Five of them agree on the value seventy-two, while three disagree with each other producing sixty-five, eighty-one and seventy-two point five. A majority vote selects seventy-two. Its properties are that errors are independent so a bad path is outvoted rather than inherited, that the traces can run at the same time so latency is one trace not eight, that it requires answers you can compare for equality, and that it fails silently when the model is systematically rather than randomly wrong. A closing bar states that sequential compute deepens one attempt while parallel compute de-risks many, and that most production systems should try the second before buying more of the first.">

::: {.fig-cap}
The two columns cost the same and are billed the same, so the choice between
them is pure engineering rather than budgeting. Note the latency asymmetry in
particular: the eight traces on the right are independent, so a server that can
batch them returns an answer in the time of *one* trace, not eight. Parallel
compute is the only way in this chapter to buy accuracy without buying wait.
:::
::::

### What the original paper found

@wang2023selfconsistency sampled 40 reasoning paths per problem and took the
majority answer. On GSM8K with PaLM-540B this moved accuracy from **56.5% with
greedy chain-of-thought decoding to 74.4%** — $+17.9$ points, from the same
model, with no retraining and no extra prompt engineering. The gains were
smaller but consistent elsewhere: on GPT-3 code-davinci-002, SVAMP rose from
75.8% to 86.8% and AQuA from 39.8% to 52.0%.[^sc-models]

[^sc-models]: Worth a footnote because it is easy to garble: the +11.0 and
+12.2 deltas quoted above are code-davinci-002, not PaLM-540B. PaLM-540B's own
SVAMP gain is $+7.6$ (79.0 → 86.6). Only the GSM8K figure of $+17.9$ happens to
hold for both models. This is the kind of detail that gets flattened in
secondary write-ups, and flattening it would make the technique look more
uniform than it is.

The number to design around, though, is not the headline. It is the **shape**.
The paper sweeps 1, 5, 10, 20 and 40 paths and reports that "in most cases the
performance saturates quickly", recommending you "try a small number of paths
(e.g., 5 or 10) ... to realize most of the gains".

That is a strong economic claim hiding in a limitations section. Cost grows
linearly in $k$ — every path is a full generation — while benefit saturates.
So the *last* sample you pay for is worth far less than the first, and there is a
$k$ beyond which you are buying nothing. Which raises the obvious question:
where is it, for a small model, on a real task?

### Our measurement: what the fifth sample is worth

Asserting that majority voting saturates is easy. The curve is rarely plotted,
so here it is. We take the first 120 of the same GSM8K problems, fix a 512-token
thinking budget, and sample $k = 5$ independent traces per problem with different
seeds. Because the sampler shuffles with a fixed seed and we take a prefix, these
120 are a genuine subset of the 200 used elsewhere. Then we compute majority@$k$
offline for every $k$ from 1 to 5, on the *same* samples — so the curve is a
property of the aggregation, not of five separate experiments with different luck.

We planned eight samples and stopped at five, which is worth reporting because
the reason is a cost this chapter had otherwise missed. **Sampled traces are
much slower per problem than greedy ones at the same budget.** The sequential
sweep managed 0.28 minutes per problem at a 512-token budget; sampling at
temperature averaged **1.43** minutes for the same work — five times the cost,
and none of it visible in the token *count*. A greedy trace often
converges and emits its stop token early; a sampled one wanders closer to the
full cap every time. Five passes over 120 problems took **14 hours**.[^slowdown]

[^slowdown]: The range is honest rather than sloppy: the first three samples
    averaged 1.15 minutes per problem and the last two 1.85, on a laptop that had
    by then been generating continuously for half a day. We cannot cleanly
    separate the sampling penalty from thermal and memory-pressure drift over a
    14-hour run, so we quote both ends. The comparison against 0.28 survives
    either way, which is the only part the argument needs.

If you budget parallel compute by multiplying the single-trace cost by $k$, you
will under-budget it — and the error compounds exactly when you are trying to
decide whether parallel is cheaper than sequential.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**This is not an equal-token comparison, and you should not read it as one.**
Each of the five samples runs at the full 512-token budget, which
@sec-budgets measured at about 755 total tokens per problem. Five of those is
roughly **3,800 tokens** — about $2.3\times$ what the 2,048-token sequential
row spends. So if majority@5 beats the deepest sequential row here, that is
*not* evidence that parallel beats sequential. It is a more expensive arm
winning, which is the least interesting way to win.

The honest version is the one @sec-reasoning-lab asks you to run: hold the token
budget fixed and split it both ways — `8 × 256` against `1 × 2048`. We report
the saturation curve because the *shape* is the point, and the shape is a
property of the aggregation at any budget. Where the two strategies cross at
equal cost is a question this run was not designed to answer.
:::

| samples $k$ | majority@$k$ | 95% CI | gain over $k=1$ | any-correct@$k$ | left on the table |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1 | 73.3% | 64.8–80.4 | +0.0 | 73.3% | 0.0 |
| 2 | 73.3% | 64.8–80.4 | +0.0 | 81.7% | 8.3 |
| 3 | 77.5% | 69.2–84.1 | +4.2 | 83.3% | 5.8 |
| 4 | 75.8% | 67.4–82.6 | +2.5 | 85.8% | 10.0 |
| 5 | 76.7% | 68.3–83.3 | +3.3 | 85.8% | 9.2 |

Three things in that table are worth more than the headline.

**First, the honest headline itself.** Five samples bought $+3.3$ points, and
that is not separable from zero:

```text
majority@1 vs majority@5, McNemar (paired, same 120 problems)
  right@1 wrong@5: 2     wrong@1 right@5: 6
  chi-sq(1) = 1.12   <  3.841        NOT separable at p = .05
```

Eight discordant problems is all $n=120$ gave us to work with. The direction is
right and matches the literature; the magnitude is not something we measured
sharply, and the curve wobbling *down* at $k=4$ before coming back up is what
noise looks like at this sample size. Self-consistency is a well-replicated
result and nothing here contradicts it — but our own run is not the evidence.

**Second, the $k=2$ row is not a fluke, and it teaches the mechanism.** Its gain
is exactly $+0.0$, and we verified it is exactly $+0.0$ per problem: majority@2
gave the same answer as majority@1 on **120 of 120**. That is structural, not
luck. With two votes you either get agreement — in which case the winner is the
answer sample 1 already gave — or a $1\!-\!1$ tie, which any implementation must
break somehow, and `collections.Counter` breaks it towards the first sample.
Either way you paid for a second full generation and mathematically could not
have changed the outcome.[^tie-break]

[^tie-break]: The specific tie-break matters less than the parity. Break ties
    randomly and $k=2$ stops being a strict no-op, but it still buys you a coin
    flip on the 28% of problems where the two samples disagree, which is not
    what anyone means by "voting". **Prefer odd $k$.** The general shape is that
    going from $2m$ to $2m{+}1$ samples buys real tie-breaking power while
    $2m{-}1$ to $2m$ buys comparatively little — visible here as the dip at
    $k=4$.

**Third — and this is the column to actually design around — look at what voting
throws away.** By $k=5$ the correct answer was somewhere in the five samples
**85.8%** of the time. Voting extracted **76.7%**. The last column is the
difference: **9.2 points that the model had already computed and paid for, and
that counting discarded.**

That gap is the entire business case for the next section. It is an upper bound
on what any re-ranking method could add on top of these same samples, it is
nearly three times what majority voting itself won, and unlike the $+3.3$ it is
not fighting for significance — on those problems the model demonstrably
produced the right answer and the aggregation step lost it. Counting is simply a
poor reader of its own evidence.

### When you can score, do not vote

Majority voting throws information away. It looks only at the *final answers*
and ignores everything the model wrote to get there. If you can build something
that judges a candidate solution, you can do better than counting.

That something is a [verifier](#gloss-verifier){#term-verifier .term-ref}: a
model trained to score solutions rather than produce them. @cobbe2021training introduced the pattern together with GSM8K
itself — sample many solutions, score each with a trained verifier, return the
best.

::: {#gloss-verifier .column-margin .term-gloss}
**verifier** — a model trained to score candidate solutions rather than to
generate them. *Outcome*-supervised verifiers judge only the final answer;
*process*-supervised ones judge each step.
[↩](#term-verifier){.term-back}
:::

Their claim about what this is *worth* is the one to remember, because it is
denominated in a currency engineers already understand: a 6B model with
verification "slightly outperforms a finetuned 175B model, thereby offering a
boost approximately equivalent to a 30x model size increase". Sampling 100
solutions and scoring them beat a model thirty times the size.

@lightman2024verify then asked what the verifier should be trained to judge, and
the answer generalises well past their setting. Scoring the *final answer* is
**outcome supervision**; scoring *each step* is **process supervision**. On a
500-problem subset of MATH, selecting the best of 1,860 samples:

| selection method | MATH problems solved |
|:--|--:|
| majority voting (self-consistency) | 69.6% |
| outcome-supervised verifier | 72.4% |
| process-supervised verifier | **78.2%** |

Read the first two rows together and the section title earns itself: a verifier
that reads the work beats a vote that only counts conclusions, at identical
sample cost. Read all three and you get the further point — *what* you supervise
is worth more than the fact that you supervised at all. The paper's explanation
is that step-level labels "provide more precise feedback than outcome
supervision", and that "the marginal value of a negative label from outcome
supervision is low": knowing a 40-step solution ended wrong tells you almost
nothing about which step to blame.

The distinction that matters in practice is **what you supervise**:

| | outcome supervision | process supervision |
|:--|:--|:--|
| the label says | the final answer was right | *this step* was right |
| labels come from | an automatic check — cheap | human annotation of steps — expensive |
| rewards | getting there | getting there *for the right reasons* |
| known failure | credits a lucky guess after broken reasoning | none that is cheap; the cost is the problem |

Outcome supervision has a specific pathology that connects straight back to
@sec-faithfulness: a solution that reasons wrongly and arrives at the right
number receives full credit. Train on enough of those and you are actively
selecting for reasoning that does not have to be sound.

### How far this actually goes

@snell2025scaling is the paper usually cited for "test-time compute beats making
the model bigger", and it is worth citing accurately, because the popular
version of the claim drops the half that constrains it.

The efficiency result is real: choosing *how* to spend test-time compute
per-question, rather than fixing one strategy, improves "the efficiency of
test-time compute scaling by more than 4× compared to a best-of-N baseline".
But the comparison against pretraining is explicitly conditional. Test-time
compute wins "on the easy questions or in settings with a lower inference load";
pretraining wins "on the harder questions or in settings with a higher inference
load". And on the hardest problems they observe "very little benefits from
scaling up test-time compute".

Their own summary is the sentence to take away: **"Test-time and pretraining
compute are not 1-to-1 'exchangeable'."**

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Both halves of that finding are useful to you.** The first says a small model
plus a good test-time strategy can serve a workload you assumed needed a large
one — which is a budget you can actually get approved. The second says this
stops working exactly where you most wanted it to, on the hard tail, and that
inference volume matters: at high enough traffic, paying once to train a better
model beats paying per-request forever.

Both halves are decisions about *your* traffic mix, not facts about models.
:::

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**All three techniques in this section need a checkable answer.** Majority
voting needs answers you can compare for equality. Verifiers need training data
in which correctness is defined. Search needs a score to search against.

For "summarise this contract", "write a polite Turkish reply to this complaint",
or "is this review positive" with a nuanced middle, none of that exists in a
usable form. **Test-time compute is easiest to buy exactly where correctness is
cheapest to check** — which is not the same set of tasks as the ones your
product is made of. Note the shape of this constraint: it is the same one that
limited *verifiable reward* training in
@sec-cot-two-ways, arriving now at inference time.
:::

### The decision, compressed

| your situation | spend it on | why |
|:--|:--|:--|
| answers are checkable, latency has slack | more parallel samples | errors are independent; the vote concentrates |
| answers are checkable, latency is tight | more parallel samples, batched | eight traces cost the time of one |
| the task needs long derivations | a longer single trace | later steps genuinely need earlier ones |
| you have labelled solutions | a verifier over samples | scoring beats counting; it reads the work |
| answers are free-form text | neither, yet | nothing here has anything to aggregate on |
| the model is *systematically* wrong | none of the above | voting amplifies bias; fix the model or the prompt |
## Where reasoning helps, and where it only burns tokens {#sec-cot-limits}

The claim this section exists to kill is the one your vendor's landing page
makes: that a reasoning model is a *better model*, and switching to it upgrades
everything you do. It does not. It upgrades a specific, identifiable, narrower
set of tasks than almost anybody expects, and on the rest it bills you for a
pile of tokens your user never reads, in exchange for output that is no better
and answers that arrive later. How much you pay for that privilege depends on
the model, the task and the budget — which is why this section ends with us
measuring it rather than quoting it.

The honest version is a question with two parts, and you can answer both before
writing any code.

### The two questions that decide it

**Does the task need serial computation?** @sec-why-tokens-compute said extra
tokens buy serial depth. So the tasks that gain are the ones where step $k$
genuinely cannot be computed until step $k-1$ is known: arithmetic over several
operations, multi-constraint scheduling, code that has to satisfy an invariant,
a proof. If a competent human would reach for scratch paper, the model probably
needs the token equivalent.

If instead the answer is a **judgement about the input as a whole** — is this
review positive, is this email spam, which of five categories is this ticket —
there is no chain. There is a pattern, and the pattern is either recognised in
one pass or it is not. Extra passes have nothing to do, and they are not
harmless: they give the model 500 tokens in which to talk itself out of a
correct first impression.

**Can you check the answer cheaply?** This one decides whether *any* of
@sec-parallel-compute is available to you — voting, verifiers, search all need
a notion of "the same answer" or "a better answer". It is independent of the
first question, and forgetting that produces most of the bad architecture
decisions in this area.

:::: {.anlp-fig}

The verdict is that test-time compute pays here and everything in this chapter is available. verifiers — is a top-row technique.

::::

### The evidence, at population scale

You do not have to take the two questions on faith. @sprague2025cot did the
arithmetic across the field: a meta-analysis of **1,218 experimental comparisons
drawn from 110 papers**, plus their own evaluation of **20 datasets across 14
models**. It is, as far as we know, the largest attempt to answer "when does
chain-of-thought actually help" with a population rather than an anecdote.

Their first finding is stated flatly enough to quote whole: **"CoT only helps
substantially on problems requiring mathematical, logical, or algorithmic
reasoning."**

The literature-wide numbers behind it:

| task category | average CoT gain |
|:--|--:|
| symbolic reasoning | $+14.2$ points |
| mathematics | $+12.3$ points |
| logical reasoning | $+6.9$ points |
| **everything else** | **$+0.7$ points** (56.8 with CoT vs 56.1 without) |

Sit with that last row. Averaged over every non-symbolic category in the
surveyed literature, chain-of-thought moved accuracy by **seven tenths of a
point** — for a multiple of the tokens. The authors' own verdict is the driest
sentence in the paper: "We do not consider this small improvement a victory for
CoT."

Nor is "no help" the worst case. Their central claim allows for the boost
"giving little to no improvement (or even hurting performance) on non-symbolic
tasks".[^sprague-arith]

[^sprague-arith]: A caution on reading those numbers together. Across the top
three categories the pooled averages are 56.9 with CoT against 45.5 without,
a gap of 11.4 points, while the mean of the three per-category deltas is 11.1.
The two are weighted differently and the paper does not reconcile them, so do
not report either as *the* average gain. The ranking is the robust finding; the
third decimal place is not.

There is a second finding that changes what you should build. Chain-of-thought,
they argue, "primarily helps with the execution step that performs computation
and symbolic manipulation, but falls short of what LLMs with tool augmentation
can do". The trap this describes is worth naming: on the problems where CoT
helps, **you usually already have something better than CoT** — a calculator, a
SQL engine, a constraint solver, a Python sandbox. And on the soft-reasoning
problems where no such tool exists, CoT does not help much either.
@sec-tool-design is the constructive version of this paragraph.

### Our measurement: the same sweep on a task with no chain in it

The cleanest way to see this is to run the *identical* experiment on a task from
the left column. So we repeat @sec-budgets — same model, same two-phase harness,
same budget ladder up to 1,024 tokens — on Turkish sentiment classification,
using the labelled review split from @sec-bake-off. (We stop at 1,024 rather
than 2,048 here. If a one-word label is not decided after a thousand tokens of
deliberation, another thousand is not the missing ingredient.)

One design note that matters. The natural split is about 94% positive, and on an
unbalanced set a model that answers `olumlu` to everything scores 94% and looks
like a genius. So we sample a **balanced** 200 examples, 100 of each class, and
report macro-F1 alongside accuracy. The prompt asks for one word:

```text
Aşağıdaki ürün yorumunun duygusu olumlu mu, olumsuz mu?
Sadece tek kelime yaz: olumlu veya olumsuz.

Yorum: "..."
```

| thinking budget | accuracy | 95% CI | macro-F1 | tokens per review | unparseable |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| none | 69.5% | 62.8–75.5 | 67.0 | 3 | 0 |
| 128 tokens | 56.5% | 49.6–63.2 | 47.8 | 127 | 4 |
| 256 tokens | 66.0% | 59.2–72.2 | 62.8 | 233 | 2 |
| 512 tokens | 72.5% | 65.9–78.2 | 71.1 | 283 | 1 |
| 1,024 tokens | 73.5% | 67.0–79.1 | 72.7 | 302 | 2 |

**Look at the token column first, because it is the one that is not ambiguous.**
Answering directly costs **3 tokens per review** — the model writes `olumlu` and
stops. The 1,024-token budget costs **302**. That is **88.6× the tokens** to put
one word on the screen.

Now the accuracy column, and here we have to be careful, because a fast reading
gets it exactly backwards. The top budget scores 73.5% against the baseline's
69.5%. That looks like thinking helping by four points — the opposite of what
this section set out to show. It is not, and this is a good place to practise
not believing your own table:

```text
vs no-thinking baseline (n=200, paired: same reviews, same seed)
                     delta      z-test         McNemar (correct test)
  budget   128:     -13.0    z = -2.69       chi-sq = 14.20   SEPARABLE
  budget   256:      -3.5    z = -0.75       chi-sq =  0.68   not separable
  budget   512:      +3.0    z = +0.66       chi-sq =  0.52   not separable
  budget  1024:      +4.0    z = +0.89       chi-sq =  0.98   not separable
```

**Exactly one row in this sweep is statistically real, and it is a harm.** The
128-token budget costs 13 points, and both tests agree emphatically — McNemar
puts it at $\chi^2 = 14.20$ against a 3.84 threshold, driven by 35 reviews the
baseline got right and thinking got wrong against only 9 in the other direction.
The apparent four-point *gain* at the top of the table is noise: $\chi^2 = 0.98$,
nowhere near separable.[^classify-mcnemar]

[^classify-mcnemar]: This sweep ran after we had fixed the harness to save
    per-problem correctness, so unlike @sec-budgets we can run McNemar here —
    the test the paired design actually calls for. It is worth seeing the two
    side by side. On the 128 row the paired test is dramatically more
    confident than the unpaired one ($\chi^2 = 14.20$, versus $z = -2.69$
    scraping past the threshold), because it throws away the ~150 reviews both
    conditions score identically and concentrates on the 44 they disagree
    about. That is the power @sec-budgets lost by saving only means.

**The truncation column explains the shape once again**, and this time it also
explains why the curve stops moving. The fraction of traces cut off runs 96%,
51%, 8.5%, 3.5%. But look at what the model actually *generates*: 124, 229, 279,
297 thinking tokens. It asks for roughly 300 tokens and then stops on its own.
Raising the ceiling from 512 to 1,024 bought 18 extra tokens of thinking and
changed nothing, which is the empirical version of the note above about not
bothering with a 2,048 row.

So the honest summary of this task is not "thinking hurts". It is sharper:

> Thinking **never significantly helped** on this task at any budget. Truncated
> thinking **significantly hurt** it. And the ceiling that stopped hurting cost
> 88.6× the tokens of not thinking at all.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**One artefact we do not have here.** @sec-budgets had to publish a caveat about
the 320-token answer cap distorting its GSM8K numbers. On this task that worry
is measurable and it is absent: mean answer length is **3 to 5 tokens** and
**0.0%** of answers hit the ceiling at any budget. The instrument is clean, so
the comparison between the two sweeps is a comparison of tasks rather than of
measurement noise. This is why the answer-cap diagnostic was worth adding even
though it arrived late — it is what lets us say the GSM8K table is suspect and
this one is not.
:::

### Longer is not monotone

There is a stronger version of this finding, and it is recent enough that it has
not reached most engineering practice: on some tasks, accuracy does not merely
*stop* improving with longer reasoning — it **declines**.

@gema2025inverse built tasks specifically to expose this, and describe the
result as an **inverse scaling relationship between test-time compute and
accuracy**: "we construct evaluation tasks where extending the reasoning length
of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) deteriorates performance". Three task families
show it — simple counting with distractors present, regression with spurious
features, and deduction under constraint tracking — alongside a separate
alignment evaluation.

The failure modes are not identical across model families, which is the detail
that makes this actionable rather than merely alarming. In their words, "Claude
models become increasingly distracted by irrelevant information as they reason
longer, while OpenAI o-series models resist distractors but show tendency to
apply memorized solution patterns when recognizing familiar problem framings
rather than genuinely reasoning through the actual question".

Two of their reported magnitudes give a sense of scale: DeepSeek R1 with five
distractors present drops "from 70% to 30%" as reasoning extends, and Claude
Opus 4 on a misleading-mathematics task falls "from nearly 100% to around
85-90%".[^inv-approx]

[^inv-approx]: These are the authors' own approximations, read from figures with
confidence intervals rather than tabulated, and we quote their hedged wording
deliberately. The direction is the finding; the decimals are not available.

This should not be mysterious after @sec-why-tokens-compute. A model given room
to keep going will keep going. If the correct answer was available at token 50,
tokens 51 through 900 are 850 opportunities to find a more interesting story:
to over-fit a distractor in the prompt, to construct an elaborate edge case, to
reconsider a correct step because reconsidering is what the trained behaviour
looks like. Extra depth is only useful if there is remaining work; otherwise it
is unconstrained generation with a spare 850 tokens.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**The cheapest experiment in this chapter.** Before enabling reasoning across a
product, run your existing evaluation set twice — once with thinking on, once
off — and compare cost per correct answer rather than accuracy. On a
classification workload this takes an afternoon and has, in our measurement,
a decent chance of telling you to leave the feature switched off.

The default to argue for is **reasoning off, enabled per-route where a
measurement says it pays** — not reasoning on, disabled where somebody
complains about the bill.
:::
## Faithfulness: a trace is not a log {#sec-faithfulness}

Here is the assumption almost everyone makes on first contact with a reasoning
model, usually without noticing they have made it: **the trace explains the
answer.** The model worked something out, the block shows the working, so
reading the block tells you why you got what you got.

It is a reasonable thing to assume. Every other place an engineer sees a
step-by-step record — a stack trace, a query plan, an audit log — the record is
*emitted by* the process it describes. The causation runs from the computation
to the text.

A reasoning trace is not built that way. The trace is **generated**, token by
token, by the same next-token machinery that generates everything else. It is
the model's continuation of the prompt, not an instrument reading. Nothing in
training requires it to name the features that actually moved the answer.
@sec-why-tokens-compute already told you this would be true: what pays is the
serial computation and the values written down, and *prose that misdescribes the
computation can sit alongside a correct answer at no cost to the objective*.

::: {#gloss-faithfulness .column-margin .term-gloss}
**faithfulness** — the degree to which a model's stated reasoning reflects the
process that actually produced its answer. A separate property from whether
either the reasoning or the answer is correct.
[↩](#term-faithfulness){.term-back}
:::

Keep this apart from accuracy. A trace can be **correct and unfaithful** (sound
steps, but not the reason for the answer) or **wrong and faithful** (the model
really did reason that badly). [Faithfulness](#gloss-faithfulness){#term-faithfulness .term-ref}
is a claim about *causation*, and you cannot read it off the page.

:::: {.anlp-fig}
```{=html}

The upper panel, labelled the assumption, shows a prompt feeding an internal computation, the computation being recorded as a reasoning trace, and the trace producing the answer. Every arrow is solid, and a caption states that the trace is a log, so the causation runs from the computation to the text, and reading the trace tells you why. The lower panel, labelled what is actually measured, shows a prompt that contains a hidden biasing feature, such as a suggested answer. The thick arrow in panel B is the whole problem. It carries most of the effect
on the answer, and it does not pass through the text you were planning to read.
Note that nothing here requires the model to be deceptive — an unfaithful trace
is the *default* outcome of training a model to produce steps that look like
